chunks: When the two angels of the sick servant ascend to the sky every evening, the Lord — Blessed and Exalted — says: 'What have the two of you written for My servant during his illness?' So they say: 'Complaints.'
So He says: 'It would not be just of Me toward My servant if I were to imprison him in one of My prisons and then forbid him from complaining.'

Then He says: 'Write for My servant the like of what you two used to write for him in goodness during his health, and do not record against him any sin until I release him from My prison, for he is indeed in a prison from My prisons.'

key_terms.الشِّكَايَة: Complaining, voicing grievances — here permitted for the sick as an expression of human weakness before God
key_terms.الْخَيْر: Good/goodness — the righteous deeds and merits continually recorded for the sick believer
key_terms.حَبْس: Prison — metaphor for illness as a divinely ordained confinement; one of God's 'prisons' (trials)
key_terms.مَا أَنْصَفْتُ: It would not be just of Me — divine declaration of fairness, emphasizing God's transcendent justice even in trials

ai.seo_question: Does illness prevent good deeds from being recorded by the angels in Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith, attributed to Imam al-Sadiq (AS), presents a vivid theological image of divine mercy extended to the sick believer. Allah describes illness as a 'prison' from His prisons — a temporary divine decree — and on this basis declares it unjust to prevent the sick from voicing complaints. He therefore commands the recording angels to continue writing the believer's good deeds as during health, and to refrain from recording sins. This teaching reassures the faithful that illness, far from being a punishment, is a form of divine custody in which the servant's spiritual record is protected and enhanced.
word_analysis: have the two of you written

en.hubeali:
A number of our companions, from Sahl Bin Ziyad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abdul Hameed, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said: ‘When the two Angels Allocated to the sick person ascend to the sky during every evening, the Lord<sup>azwj</sup> Blessed and High is Saying: “What is that which the two of you have written for My<sup>azwj</sup> servant during his illness?” So they are saying: ‘The complaints’.

So He<sup>azwj</sup> is Saying: “There would not be justice for My<sup>azwj</sup> servant if I<sup>azwj</sup> were to Imprison him in a prison of My<sup>azwj</sup> prisons, then Forbid him from complaining.

Write down for My<sup>azwj</sup> servant the like of what you two would have written for him from the goodness during his good health, and do not write sins against him until I<sup>azwj</sup> Release him from My<sup>azwj</sup> prison, for he is in a prison from My<sup>azwj</sup> prisons”’.
en.sarwar: 5. A number of our people have narrated from Sahl ibn Ziyad from ibn Mahbub from ‘Abd al-Hamid who has said the following: “Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said that when the two guard angels of a person suffering from illness ascend to heavens every evening, the Lord, Most Holy, Most Blessed, asks them, ‘What did you write down for My servant in his illness?’ They will say, ‘We wrote down his complaints.’
